name: Lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus)
definition: A long-term autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks healthy tissue, most often causing joint aches, skin rashes and tiredness.
overview: Lupus is a lasting autoimmune illness in which the immune system attacks healthy tissue. It is most often marked by joint aches, skin rashes and fatigue, and symptoms vary from person to person and can come and go. It is more common in women. There is no cure, but symptoms can improve if treatment starts early.
causes: Autoimmune: the immune system attacks healthy tissue
Possible contributors named by the NHS include viral infections, certain medicines, sunlight, puberty, childbirth and the menopause
riskFactors: Being of African, Caribbean, Asian or Chinese background
Developing it before the age of 50 is typical
signs: A rash across the nose and cheeks, sometimes called a butterfly rash
Painful, swollen joints with morning stiffness
A high level of a certain type of antibody on blood tests
complications: In severe cases, serious inflammation of the heart, lungs, brain or kidneys
Lupus nephritis (kidney inflammation), which in a few cases can progress to kidney failure
Pre-eclampsia and premature birth, which are more likely when lupus is active in early pregnancy
diagnosis: No single test confirms lupus, so doctors combine the person's history, a physical examination and laboratory tests. A GP usually starts with blood tests, and lupus may be diagnosed if they show a high level of a certain type of antibody together with typical symptoms. Blood counts, kidney function tests, urine protein checks and sometimes a tissue biopsy may also be used. Imaging of the heart, kidneys or other organs may follow if they seem affected.
treatment: There is no cure, and care is tailored to the person's symptoms, aiming to control them and to prevent, limit and stop flares. The NHS lists anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen, hydroxychloroquine for fatigue, skin and joint problems, and steroids for kidney inflammation and rashes. Immunosuppressant or biological medicines may be used for severe cases. Self-care includes sun protection, pacing yourself, staying active and managing stress.
prevention: The NHS describes self-care that includes sun protection, pacing and managing stress. The sources reviewed did not describe a way to prevent lupus itself.
seekCare: A routine GP appointment is the usual route if joint pain, rashes or extreme tiredness keep coming back, since lupus is easier to manage when found early. Seizures, new weakness, vision problems or chest pain on deep breathing call for prompt medical assessment: NHS 111 or the GP the same day, and call 999 if they are severe or sudden.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of lupus?
sections.body:
Lupus symptoms vary widely from person to person and can come and go. The NHS lists joint and muscle pain and extreme tiredness that does not go away however much a person rests as main symptoms. A rash often appears across the nose and cheeks and can get worse in sunlight. NIAMS describes this as a butterfly-shaped rash.

Other possible signs include headaches, mouth ulcers, fever, hair loss, weight loss and swollen glands. Some people have Raynaud's, where the fingers and toes change colour. Arthritis in lupus can cause painful, swollen joints and morning stiffness. Lupus can also affect organs such as the kidneys, heart, lungs and brain. Early symptoms can be mistaken for another type of inflammatory arthritis and may appear months or years before a diagnosis.

sections.heading: What causes lupus and who gets it?
sections.body:
Lupus is an autoimmune condition, which means the immune system attacks healthy tissue. It is not contagious. The exact trigger is unclear, but the NHS lists possible contributors including viral infections, certain medicines, sunlight, puberty, childbirth and the menopause. Unusual antibodies that react against the body's own tissue are found in the blood, and the resulting inflammation can damage tissues.

Lupus is more common in women, and the NHS says it is more common in people of African, Caribbean, Asian or Chinese background. A hospital rheumatology service says it is about nine times more common in women than in men and tends to develop before the age of 50. A local NHS guideline describes the condition as rare.

sections.heading: How is lupus diagnosed?
sections.body:
Because the symptoms overlap with other conditions, diagnosis can take time. No single test confirms lupus, and doctors combine the person's history, a physical examination and laboratory tests. Symptoms also change over time, so lupus can be misdiagnosed.

A GP usually starts with blood tests. The ANA test is often the first step, but a positive result alone does not confirm lupus because healthy people can also test positive. Doctors may also order blood counts, kidney function tests and urine protein checks, and sometimes a tissue biopsy. Imaging of the heart, kidneys or other organs may follow if they seem to be affected. The NHS says lupus may be diagnosed if tests show a high level of a certain type of antibody and the person also has the typical symptoms.

sections.heading: How is lupus treated?
sections.body:
There is no cure for lupus, but the NHS says symptoms can improve if treatment starts early. NIAMS says care is tailored to symptoms and aims to manage them and to prevent, limit and stop flares.

Options named by the NHS include anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen, hydroxychloroquine for fatigue, skin and joint problems, and steroids for kidney inflammation and rashes. For severe cases, immunosuppressant or biological medicines may be used. NIAMS says doctors generally use corticosteroids at the lowest effective dose because of their side effects. Severe involvement of the heart, lungs, kidneys and other organs often needs specialist care. NIAMS stresses that medicines should not be stopped without medical advice.

sections.heading: Living with lupus: flares and self-care
sections.body:
Flares, when symptoms worsen, range from mild to serious and do not follow a pattern. Lupus UK describes a flare as a time when the disease becomes active and symptoms worsen or new ones appear, with quieter periods in between. NIAMS says learning a person's own warning signs helps, and that many people with lupus live satisfying and productive lives.

The NHS self-care advice includes sun protection, pacing yourself, staying active and managing stress. Sun protection includes a high-factor sunscreen and a hat. Other advice includes not smoking and eating a balanced diet with vitamin D and calcium. Regular visits to the doctor are emphasised. A Lupus UK-linked summary says hormonal contraceptives containing oestrogen are generally avoided because they can provoke a flare.

sections.heading: What complications can lupus cause?
sections.body:
Severity varies, and a severe case can cause serious inflammation of the heart, lungs, brain or kidneys. Lupus nephritis is inflammation of the kidneys, and Great Ormond Street Hospital says it can in a few cases progress to kidney failure. Kidney involvement often gives no symptoms, so it is found through urine and blood tests.

Lupus UK says an increased risk of miscarriage is a complication of lupus, and that many women with lupus have healthy pregnancies when planned. Serious pregnancy complications such as pre-eclampsia and premature birth are more likely when lupus is active in early pregnancy. Heart involvement in pregnancy is mainly linked to certain antibodies, and women with anti-Ro or anti-La antibodies face a small risk of their baby developing congenital heart block.

faqs.a: No, lupus is not contagious. It is an autoimmune condition, in which the immune system attacks healthy tissue. The exact trigger is unclear, but the NHS lists possible contributors including viral infections, certain medicines, sunlight, puberty, childbirth and the menopause. These are possible contributors to developing lupus, not ways of catching it from another person.

There is no cure for lupus, according to the NHS and NIAMS. The NHS says symptoms can improve if treatment starts early. NIAMS says treatment has improved and many people manage lupus well. The NHS lists anti-inflammatory painkillers, hydroxychloroquine and steroids, with immunosuppressant or biological medicines for severe cases.

faqs.q: What is the outlook for people with lupus?
faqs.a: One source reports that the outlook for survival has improved in recent years and that most people with lupus continue to have relatively mild disease. A smaller group has more serious disease that is harder to control, particularly when the kidneys, nervous system or blood vessels are involved. A rheumatologist or lupus specialist can discuss what this means for an individual.

faqs.q: Can women with lupus have a baby?
faqs.a: Lupus UK says many women with lupus have healthy pregnancies and that planning matters. Serious complications such as pre-eclampsia and premature birth are more likely when lupus is active in early pregnancy. Lupus UK also notes an increased risk of miscarriage. Pregnancy decisions are usually discussed with a rheumatologist or lupus specialist.

faqs.q: When should I see a doctor about possible lupus?
faqs.a: NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP if lupus symptoms occur often, and notes that lupus is better managed when it is found and treated early. Joint and muscle pain, extreme tiredness that rest does not ease, and a rash across the nose and cheeks are among the main symptoms. A routine GP appointment is the usual first step, and seizures, new weakness or vision problems need prompt assessment through NHS 111 or 999.
